claim: Gastrointestinal (GI) colonization by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is associated with a high risk of transmission and invasive disease in vulnerable populations.
source: Gastrointestinal (GI) colonization by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is associated with a high risk of transmission and invasive disease in vulnerable populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature establishing the clinical significance of MRSA GI colonization.

claim: Male sex is correlated with enhanced Staphylococcus aureus nasal carriage, skin and soft tissue infections, and bacterial sepsis.
source: Male sex is correlated with enhanced Staphylococcus aureus nasal carriage, skin and soft tissue infections, and bacterial sepsis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Nowak et al., 2017; Humphreys et al., 2015; Castleman et al., 2018; Tacconelli and Foschi, 2017) establishing the correlation between male sex and S. aureus infections.

claim: Female mice rapidly cleared MRSA from the GI tract following oral inoculation in a manner dependent on the gut microbiota.
source: Our results show that in contrast to male mice that were susceptible to persistent colonization, female mice rapidly cleared MRSA from the GI tract following oral inoculation in a manner dependent on the gut microbiota.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential MRSA clearance between male and female mice, and loss of this effect in germ-free mice.

claim: Colonization resistance displayed by female mice was mediated by an increase in IL-17A+ CD4+ T cells (Th17) and dependent on neutrophils.
source: This colonization resistance displayed by female mice was mediated by an increase in IL-17A+ CD4+ T cells (Th17) and dependent on neutrophils.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing increased Th17 cells in females and experiments with knockout mice and antibody depletion studies.

claim: Ovariectomy of female mice increased MRSA burden.
source: Ovariectomy of female mice increased MRSA burden, but gonadal female mice that have the Y chromosome retained enhanced Th17 responses and colonization resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ovariectomy experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Gonadal female mice that have the Y chromosome retained enhanced Th17 responses and colonization resistance.
source: Ovariectomy of female mice increased MRSA burden, but gonadal female mice that have the Y chromosome retained enhanced Th17 responses and colonization resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from four core genotype mice showing XY(-Sry) females clear MRSA similarly to XX females.

claim: MRSA is a major global health concern due to its multidrug resistance, wide range of infections, and high morbidity and mortality rates.
source: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a major global health concern due to its multidrug resistance, wide range of infections, and high morbidity and mortality rates (David and Daum, 2010; Seybold et al., 2006; Boucher and Corey, 2008; de Kraker et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature establishing MRSA as a major health concern.

claim: Gastrointestinal S. aureus colonization is present in an estimated 20% of the healthy population.
source: Gastrointestinal (GI) S. aureus colonization is present in an estimated 20% of the healthy population (Acton et al., 2009; Gagnaire et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: An estimated 1–6% of the population are persistently colonized with MRSA.
source: and an estimated 1–6% are persistently colonized with MRSA (Acton et al., 2009; Gagnaire et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: MRSA carriage increases the likelihood of invasive infections, especially while in the hospital or post discharge.
source: MRSA carriage increases the likelihood of invasive infections, especially while in the hospital or post discharge (Huang, 2019; von Eiff et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Intestinal carriage is associated with higher rates of infections and bacteremia than nasal carriage alone.
source: Intestinal carriage is associated with higher rates of infections and bacteremia than nasal carriage alone (de Kraker et al., 2011; Squier et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies comparing intestinal and nasal carriage.

claim: The risk of transmission to other individuals in the hospital and community settings through fomite spread is increased by intestinal carriage.
source: The risk of transmission to other individuals in the hospital and community settings through fomite spread is increased by intestinal carriage (Boyce et al., 2007; Bhalla et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on MRSA transmission.

claim: High free testosterone levels are a risk factor for S. aureus throat carriage in women.
source: High free testosterone levels are a risk factor for S. aureus throat carriage in women (Nowak et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Sex steroid hormones and sex chromosomes can modulate the scale and type of immune response.
source: Sex steroid hormones and sex chromosomes can modulate the scale and type of immune response (Schurz et al., 2019; Klein and Flanagan, 2016; Jaillon et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles on sex differences in immunity.

claim: Sex hormones such as estrogen and testosterone can directly influence immune cell activation, proliferation, and cytokine response through receptor signaling.
source: Sex hormones such as estrogen and testosterone can directly influence immune cell activation, proliferation, and cytokine response through receptor signaling (Vázquez-Martínez et al., 2018; Dias et al., 2022; Fuseini et al., 2019; Chi et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on hormone-immune interactions.

claim: Males are more susceptible to GI and respiratory infections.
source: In general, males are more susceptible to GI and respiratory infections, whereas females are more affected by autoimmune diseases in part due to the pro-inflammatory effect of estradiol, but these responses are tissue and cell specific (Klein and Flanagan, 2016; Vázquez-Martínez et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles on sex differences in infection susceptibility.

claim: Females are more affected by autoimmune diseases in part due to the pro-inflammatory effect of estradiol.
source: In general, males are more susceptible to GI and respiratory infections, whereas females are more affected by autoimmune diseases in part due to the pro-inflammatory effect of estradiol, but these responses are tissue and cell specific (Klein and Flanagan, 2016; Vázquez-Martínez et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles on sex differences in autoimmunity.

claim: Previous studies examining GI MRSA colonization in mice generally rely on depletion of the mouse microbiota with antibiotics to establish long-term colonization.
source: These studies generally rely on depletion of the mouse microbiota with antibiotics to establish long-term colonization (Misawa et al., 2015; Kernbauer et al., 2015; Gries et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous mouse colonization studies.

claim: Inbred laboratory mice from different sources can display substantial differences in mucosal immune responses and susceptibility to GI colonization by microorganisms.
source: We and others have shown that inbred laboratory mice from different sources, or even the same institution, can display substantial differences in mucosal immune responses and susceptibility to GI colonization by microorganisms (Jang et al., 2023; Ramanan et al., 2014; Cadwell et al., 2010; Moon et al., 2015; Ivanov et al., 2009; Mamantopoulos et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies demonstrating variability in mouse immune responses based on source.

claim: Adult B6 mice received a single oral gavage with 10^8 colony forming units (CFU) of MRSA USA300 LAC.
source: Adult B6 mice received a single oral gavage with 108 colony forming units (CFU) of MRSA USA300 LAC, the predominant MRSA clone responsible for community-associated MRSA infections and a growing number of hospital-acquired infections in the United States (Seybold et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used in the study.

claim: MRSA USA300 LAC is the predominant MRSA clone responsible for community-associated MRSA infections and a growing number of hospital-acquired infections in the United States.
source: Adult B6 mice received a single oral gavage with 108 colony forming units (CFU) of MRSA USA300 LAC, the predominant MRSA clone responsible for community-associated MRSA infections and a growing number of hospital-acquired infections in the United States (Seybold et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on MRSA epidemiology.

claim: Mice inoculated with MRSA do not display signs of disease such as weight loss.
source: We confirmed that mice inoculated with MRSA do not display signs of disease such as weight loss (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Extraintestinal dissemination of bacteria was not observed in mice inoculated with MRSA.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Zhou et al., 2024), we did not observe extraintestinal dissemination of bacteria or histological signs of intestinal inflammation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citation to previous work.

claim: Histological signs of intestinal inflammation were not observed in mice inoculated with MRSA.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Zhou et al., 2024), we did not observe extraintestinal dissemination of bacteria or histological signs of intestinal inflammation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D and citation to previous work.

claim: In JAX mice, 10^4–10^5 CFU per gram of stool of MRSA was detected on day 2 that remained stable for at least 35 days post inoculation.
source: In JAX mice, we detected 104–105 CFU per gram of stool of MRSA on day 2 that remained stable for at least 35 days post inoculation (dpi) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: NYU mice displayed bimodal distribution of MRSA colonization data where some mice remained stably colonized while detectable MRSA burden diminished rapidly in others.
source: However, we noticed bimodal distribution of the data for NYU mice where some mice remained stably colonized while detectable MRSA burden diminished rapidly in others.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from the colonization data.

claim: NYU mice that displayed resistance to MRSA colonization were females.
source: Segregation of the groups by sex revealed that NYU mice that displayed resistance to MRSA colonization were females.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data when mice were segregated by sex.

claim: Male NYU mice displayed sustained colonization at levels similar to male and female JAX mice.
source: Despite originating from the same litters, male NYU mice displayed sustained colonization at levels similar to male and female JAX mice, while MRSA levels were already lower by day 2 and undetectable by 2–3 weeks post inoculation in female NYU mice (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: MRSA levels were already lower by day 2 and undetectable by 2–3 weeks post inoculation in female NYU mice.
source: Despite originating from the same litters, male NYU mice displayed sustained colonization at levels similar to male and female JAX mice, while MRSA levels were already lower by day 2 and undetectable by 2–3 weeks post inoculation in female NYU mice (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Commensal microbes that are constituents of the microbiota can inhibit S. aureus nasal, skin, and intestinal colonization.
source: Commensal microbes that are constituents of the microbiota can inhibit S. aureus nasal, skin, and intestinal colonization (Piewngam et al., 2018; Krismer et al., 2017; Nakatsuji et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on microbiota-mediated colonization resistance.

claim: Stable MRSA GI colonization was observed in germ-free mice of both sexes.
source: In support of a role for commensal microbes in promoting colonization resistance in NYU female mice, we observed stable MRSA GI colonization in germ-free (GF) mice of both sexes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Sustained MRSA GI colonization and no sex difference was observed in minimal flora mice colonized with Oligo-MM12+FA3.
source: We observed sustained MRSA GI colonization and no sex difference in these minimal flora mice, indicating that additional intestinal commensals contribute to sex-dependent colonization resistance (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Additional intestinal commensals beyond the Oligo-MM12+FA3 consortium contribute to sex-dependent colonization resistance.
source: We observed sustained MRSA GI colonization and no sex difference in these minimal flora mice, indicating that additional intestinal commensals contribute to sex-dependent colonization resistance (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that minimal flora mice lack sex-dependent colonization resistance.

claim: JAX female mice cleared MRSA colonization similarly to NYU female mice when co-housed together.
source: When housed together, JAX female mice cleared MRSA colonization similarly to their NYU cage mates (Figure 1F and G), indicating that the microbiota of NYU female mice promotes resistance to colonization and that this protective property can be transferred.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: The microbiota of NYU female mice promotes resistance to colonization and this protective property can be transferred.
source: When housed together, JAX female mice cleared MRSA colonization similarly to their NYU cage mates (Figure 1F and G), indicating that the microbiota of NYU female mice promotes resistance to colonization and that this protective property can be transferred.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-housing experiment results shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Samples from 16S sequencing were distinguished based on the source of mice (NYU vs JAX) rather than sex.
source: Principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) of operational taxonomic units (OTUs) showed that samples were distinguished based on the source of mice (NYU vs JAX) rather than sex (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCoA analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Overall alpha diversity as measured by Shannon index was increased in JAX mice compared to NYU mice prior to MRSA inoculation.
source: Overall alpha diversity as measured by Shannon index was increased in JAX mice compared to NYU mice prior to MRSA inoculation, as well as in JAX females compared to NYU females (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Shannon index analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Alpha diversity by Shannon index between NYU males and females shows a similar spread when comparing sexes.
source: Alpha diversity by Shannon index between NYU males and females shows a similar spread when comparing sexes (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Shannon index analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: JAX females had higher abundance of Clostridiaceae and Lachnospiraceae family members.
source: JAX females had higher abundance of Clostridiaceae and Lachnospiraceae family members, while NYU female microbiomes were dominated by the Muribaculaceae family (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by taxonomic abundance data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: NYU female microbiomes were dominated by the Muribaculaceae family.
source: JAX females had higher abundance of Clostridiaceae and Lachnospiraceae family members, while NYU female microbiomes were dominated by the Muribaculaceae family (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by taxonomic abundance data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The NYU male and female microbiomes clustered together.
source: The NYU male and female microbiomes clustered together (Figure 2A) and had similar relative taxonomic abundances (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCoA analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NYU male and female microbiomes had similar relative taxonomic abundances.
source: The NYU male and female microbiomes clustered together (Figure 2A) and had similar relative taxonomic abundances (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by taxonomic abundance data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The observed sex bias in colonization resistance may not be due to microbiome composition alone.
source: These findings suggest that the observed sex bias in colonization resistance may not be due to microbiome composition alone.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that NYU males and females have similar microbiome composition but different colonization outcomes.

claim: JAX female mice receiving an FMT from NYU female, but not male donor mice, displayed colonization resistance to MRSA.
source: JAX female mice receiving an FMT from NYU female, but not male donor mice, displayed colonization resistance to MRSA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FMT experiments.

claim: An FMT using NYU female donor stool was unable to confer colonization resistance to JAX male recipients.
source: However, an FMT using NYU female donor stool was unable to confer colonization resistance to JAX male recipients (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The microbiota contributes to the difference between female JAX and NYU mice.
source: Therefore, the microbiota contributes to the difference between female JAX and NYU mice, but other factors mediate the divergence of female and male NYU mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the FMT experiments showing that microbiota transfer can confer resistance to JAX females but not to males.

claim: Other factors beyond microbiota mediate the divergence of female and male NYU mice.
source: Therefore, the microbiota contributes to the difference between female JAX and NYU mice, but other factors mediate the divergence of female and male NYU mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the FMT experiments showing that microbiota transfer alone is insufficient to confer resistance to males.

claim: 795 genes were upregulated in both male and female mice following MRSA inoculation in the lamina propria.
source: In the lamina propria, 795 genes were upregulated in both male and female mice following MRSA inoculation, with an additional 352 genes upregulated in females only and 648 genes upregulated in males only, as determined by a log2 fold change cutoff of 1.2 and a false discovery rate of 0.05 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 352 genes were upregulated in females only following MRSA inoculation in the lamina propria.
source: In the lamina propria, 795 genes were upregulated in both male and female mice following MRSA inoculation, with an additional 352 genes upregulated in females only and 648 genes upregulated in males only, as determined by a log2 fold change cutoff of 1.2 and a false discovery rate of 0.05 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 648 genes were upregulated in males only following MRSA inoculation in the lamina propria.
source: In the lamina propria, 795 genes were upregulated in both male and female mice following MRSA inoculation, with an additional 352 genes upregulated in females only and 648 genes upregulated in males only, as determined by a log2 fold change cutoff of 1.2 and a false discovery rate of 0.05 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Genes with the largest downregulation following MRSA inoculation in both sexes included those involved with immunoglobulins (Ighv1-19, Igkv4-91, Bcam), cytochrome p450 genes (Cyp1a1, Cyp1b1), and von Willebrand factor (Vwf).
source: Following MRSA inoculation in both sexes, genes with the largest downregulation included those involved with immunoglobulins (Ighv1-19, Igkv4-91, Bcam), cytochrome p450 genes (Cyp1a1, Cyp1b1), and von Willebrand factor (Vwf), a secreted protein that MRSA binds to disrupt platelet recruitment and coagulation (Steinert et al., 2020; Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: von Willebrand factor (Vwf) is a secreted protein that MRSA binds to disrupt platelet recruitment and coagulation.
source: Following MRSA inoculation in both sexes, genes with the largest downregulation included those involved with immunoglobulins (Ighv1-19, Igkv4-91, Bcam), cytochrome p450 genes (Cyp1a1, Cyp1b1), and von Willebrand factor (Vwf), a secreted protein that MRSA binds to disrupt platelet recruitment and coagulation (Steinert et al., 2020; Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on Vwf function.

claim: Constitutive cytochrome P4501A1 (Cyp1a1) expression impairs the intestinal immune response against enteric pathogens.
source: Interestingly, constitutive cytochrome P4501A1 (Cyp1a1) expression impairs the intestinal immune response against enteric pathogens (Schiering et al., 2017), and its downregulation in mice inoculated with MRSA may be supportive of a mucosal immune response.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on Cyp1a1 function.

claim: Downregulation of Cyp1a1 in mice inoculated with MRSA may be supportive of a mucosal immune response.
source: Interestingly, constitutive cytochrome P4501A1 (Cyp1a1) expression impairs the intestinal immune response against enteric pathogens (Schiering et al., 2017), and its downregulation in mice inoculated with MRSA may be supportive of a mucosal immune response.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the known function of Cyp1a1 and its observed downregulation.

claim: Genes that were upregulated in the lamina propria following MRSA inoculation included those involved in T cell and neutrophil activity such as Ccl28, Sectm1b, S100g, Lrrc19, and H2-q1.
source: Genes that were upregulated in the lamina propria following MRSA inoculation included those involved in T cell and neutrophil activity such as Ccl28 (Mohan et al., 2017), Sectm1b (Huyton et al., 2011), S100g (Donato, 2007), Lrrc19 (Cao et al., 2016), and H2-q1 (Anderson and Brossay, 2016; Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A and citations to literature on gene functions.

claim: Both males and females have downregulation of immune-related Th1, Th2, and granzyme A signaling pathways following MRSA inoculation.
source: Pathway analysis of the lamina propria fraction indicated that both males and females have downregulation of immune-related Th1, Th2, and granzyme A signaling pathways, and upregulation of oxidative phosphorylation, neutrophil extracellular trap formation, glucose metabolism, and xenobiotic metabolism pathways (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both males and females have upregulation of oxidative phosphorylation, neutrophil extracellular trap formation, glucose metabolism, and xenobiotic metabolism pathways following MRSA inoculation.
source: Pathway analysis of the lamina propria fraction indicated that both males and females have downregulation of immune-related Th1, Th2, and granzyme A signaling pathways, and upregulation of oxidative phosphorylation, neutrophil extracellular trap formation, glucose metabolism, and xenobiotic metabolism pathways (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Downregulation of interleukin (IL)-4 and IL-13 pathway and upregulation of retinoid X receptor and the pregnane X receptor pathways were specific to female mice.
source: Downregulation of interleukin (IL)-4 and IL-13 pathway and upregulation of retinoid X receptor and the pregnane X receptor pathways were specific to female mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Downregulation of IL-5, IL-3, and GM-CSF signaling, and upregulation of the pyroptosis and ion channel transport pathways were unique to male mice.
source: Unique to male mice was the downregulation of IL-5, IL-3, and GM-CSF signaling, and upregulation of the pyroptosis and ion channel transport pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: There were 13 genes differentially expressed in the intestinal lamina propria between male and female mice in the MRSA condition.
source: In the MRSA condition, there were 13 genes differentially expressed in the intestinal lamina propria between male and female mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis comparing males and females.

claim: Glycosylation-dependent cell adhesion molecule-1 (Glycam1), which mediates lymphocyte trafficking to lymphoid tissues, was upregulated in female mice.
source: Glycosylation-dependent cell adhesion molecule-1 (Glycam1), which mediates lymphocyte trafficking to lymphoid tissues (Brustein et al., 1992), was upregulated in female mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D and citation to literature on Glycam1 function.

claim: Genes selectively upregulated in male mice 2 dpi included Complement protein C7 and several immunoglobulin heavy chain variants (Ighv5-4, Ighv1-49, Ighv8-5).
source: Genes selectively upregulated in male mice 2 dpi included Complement protein C7 and several immunoglobulin heavy chain variants (Ighv5-4, Ighv1-49, Ighv8-5).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data comparing males and females.

claim: Only 15 genes were upregulated in males 2 dpi with MRSA in the intestinal epithelial fraction, while 2037 were upregulated in females with no overlap between sexes.
source: In the intestinal epithelial fraction, we observed only 15 genes upregulated in males 2 dpi with MRSA, while 2037 were upregulated in females with no overlap between sexes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Female Nlrp3−/− mice displayed similar resistance to MRSA GI colonization as female Nlrp3+/− controls.
source: However, we did not observe sex-specific differences in NLRP3-associated transcripts with RNA-seq (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B) and female Nlrp3−/− mice displayed similar resistance to MRSA GI colonization as female Nlrp3+/− controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The mechanism of sex-specific resistance to MRSA colonization of the GI tract may be different from that observed during a skin infection.
source: Thus, the mechanism of sex-specific resistance to MRSA colonization of the GI tract may be different from that observed during a skin infection where barrier breach triggers an exaggerated innate immune response that may cause more harm than benefit.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that NLRP3 is not involved in GI colonization resistance but is involved in skin infection.

claim: There was no difference in MRSA burden between male Rag2−/− and Rag2+/− controls.
source: We observed no difference in burden between male Rag2−/− and Rag2+/− controls (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Female Rag2−/− mice had significantly increased MRSA burden compared to Rag2+/− littermates.
source: However, female Rag2−/− mice had significantly increased MRSA burden compared to Rag2+/− littermates (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A B or T cell-mediated response is required for the sex bias in colonization resistance.
source: These data suggest that a B or T cell-mediated response is required for the sex bias we observe in colonization resistance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Rag2 knockout experiments showing loss of sex bias in females lacking B and T cells.

claim: Ighm−/− (μMT) mice, which lack mature B lymphocytes, were similar to Ighm+/− controls and retained sex differences.
source: However, Ighm−/− (μMT) mice, which lack mature B lymphocytes, were similar to Ighm+/− controls and retained sex differences; males displayed prolonged colonization and females were resistant (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Antibody-mediated depletion of CD4+ T cells substantially increased MRSA GI colonization of female mice.
source: In contrast, antibody-mediated depletion of CD4+ T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) substantially increased MRSA GI colonization of female mice, similar to Rag2−/− mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CD4+ T cells are required for MRSA colonization resistance associated with female sex.
source: Therefore, CD4+ T cells are required for MRSA colonization resistance associated with female sex.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the CD4 depletion experiments showing loss of colonization resistance in females.

claim: Clearance of MRSA nasal colonization is mediated by neutrophil influx downstream of the type 17 response, which includes interleukin-17A (IL-17A) producing lymphoid cells such as Th17 cells.
source: In mouse models of nasal colonization, clearance is mediated by neutrophil influx downstream of the type 17 response, which includes interleukin-17A (IL-17A) producing lymphoid cells such as Th17 cells (Archer et al., 2013; Archer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on nasal colonization models.

claim: The total numbers of CD4+ T cells were similar across conditions.
source: Although the total numbers of CD4+ T cells were similar across conditions, we observed an increase in IL-17A+ CD4+ T cells in the small intestine and colon of female mice 2 dpi with MRSA that was not observed in males (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: An increase in IL-17A+ CD4+ T cells was observed in the small intestine and colon of female mice 2 dpi with MRSA that was not observed in males.
source: Although the total numbers of CD4+ T cells were similar across conditions, we observed an increase in IL-17A+ CD4+ T cells in the small intestine and colon of female mice 2 dpi with MRSA that was not observed in males (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: There were no differences in γδ T cells and innate lymphoid cells or the proportion of these lymphoid subsets that were IL-17A+.
source: There were no differences in γδ T cells and innate lymphoid cells or the proportion of these lymphoid subsets that were IL-17A+ (Figure 5C and D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C and D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: There was no difference in MRSA burden between male Rorc +/− and Rorc−/− mice that remained colonized.
source: Although there was no difference in MRSA burden between male Rorc +/− and Rorc−/− mice that remained colonized, female Rorc−/− mice had higher MRSA burden compared to Rorc +/− controls (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Female Rorc−/− mice had higher MRSA burden compared to Rorc +/− controls.
source: Although there was no difference in MRSA burden between male Rorc +/− and Rorc−/− mice that remained colonized, female Rorc−/− mice had higher MRSA burden compared to Rorc +/− controls (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Female mice deficient in the IL-17 receptor (IL-17ra) had increased MRSA burden compared to heterozygous littermates.
source: Responses to IL-17 itself was required, because female mice deficient in the IL-17 receptor (IL-17ra) had increased MRSA burden compared to heterozygous littermates (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: There was no difference in MRSA burden between Tcrd−/− and Tcrd+/− male or female mice.
source: There was no difference in MRSA burden between Tcrd−/− and Tcrd+/− male or female mice (Figure 5G), confirming that γδ T cells were not required for colonization resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: γδ T cells were not required for colonization resistance.
source: There was no difference in MRSA burden between Tcrd−/− and Tcrd+/− male or female mice (Figure 5G), confirming that γδ T cells were not required for colonization resistance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Tcrd knockout experiments showing no effect on colonization resistance.

claim: Th17 cells and IL-17 can recruit and promote antimicrobial functions of neutrophils.
source: Th17 cells and IL-17 can recruit and promote antimicrobial functions of neutrophils (McGeachy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on Th17-neutrophil interactions.

claim: Neutrophils from female mice and humans display signs of increased maturity and activation.
source: Neutrophils from female mice and humans display signs of increased maturity and activation (Blazkova et al., 2017; Er-Lukowiak et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on sex differences in neutrophil function.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the number of neutrophils between conditions.
source: Although we did not observe significant differences in the number of neutrophils between conditions (Figure 5H), neutrophils from female mice 2 dpi with MRSA had increased levels of CD11b, a sign of activation (Parkos et al., 1994), compared to males (Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Neutrophils from female mice 2 dpi with MRSA had increased levels of CD11b, a sign of activation, compared to males.
source: Although we did not observe significant differences in the number of neutrophils between conditions (Figure 5H), neutrophils from female mice 2 dpi with MRSA had increased levels of CD11b, a sign of activation (Parkos et al., 1994), compared to males (Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5I and citation to literature on CD11b as an activation marker.

claim: Antibody-mediated depletion of neutrophils led to increased MRSA burden compared with isotype control-treated mice.
source: Antibody-mediated depletion of neutrophils (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E) led to increased MRSA burden compared with isotype control-treated mice (Figure 5J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Neutrophil depletion in female mice led to an earlier and more pronounced increase in MRSA colonization that was prolonged.
source: Although colonization was increased in males, neutrophil depletion in female mice led to an earlier and more pronounced increase in MRSA colonization that was prolonged.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing neutrophil depletion effects in males and females.

claim: Neutrophils control bacterial burden to some degree but fail to promote clearance in males.
source: It is likely that neutrophils control bacterial burden to some degree but fail to promote clearance in males.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the neutrophil depletion experiments showing increased burden in both sexes but more pronounced effect in females.

claim: Neutrophils are required for clearance of MRSA in the gut of female mice.
source: In contrast, neutrophils are required for clearance of MRSA in the gut of female mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the neutrophil depletion experiments showing loss of clearance in females.

claim: Many X linked genes are involved in immunity, such as pattern recognition receptors.
source: Many X linked genes are involved in immunity, such as pattern recognition receptors, and incomplete X inactivation can lead to higher expression of such genes (Schurz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on X-linked immune genes.

claim: Incomplete X inactivation can lead to higher expression of X-linked immune genes.
source: Many X linked genes are involved in immunity, such as pattern recognition receptors, and incomplete X inactivation can lead to higher expression of such genes (Schurz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on X chromosome inactivation.

claim: Female mice that received female donor BM were resistant to MRSA.
source: Although female mice that received female donor BM were resistant to MRSA, male mice that received male or female donor BM remained colonized (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Male mice that received male or female donor BM remained colonized.
source: Although female mice that received female donor BM were resistant to MRSA, male mice that received male or female donor BM remained colonized (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: It is unlikely that a gene expressed on a sex chromosome in immune cells such as T cells mediates colonization resistance in females.
source: Thus, it is unlikely that a gene expressed on a sex chromosome in immune cells such as T cells mediates colonization resistance in females, raising the possibility of a role for sex hormones in our model.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the bone marrow chimera experiments showing that female immune cells in male hosts do not confer resistance.

claim: The hormones estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone are known to modulate trafficking and function of immune cells.
source: The hormones estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone are known to modulate trafficking and function of immune cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge on hormone-immune interactions.

claim: Estrogen can enhance responses to extracellular pathogens.
source: For example, estrogen can enhance responses to extracellular pathogens (Fuseini et al., 2019; Yasuda et al., 2019; Békési et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on estrogen's effects on immune responses.

claim: OVX mice had increased MRSA burden and duration of carriage compared to SO controls.
source: OVX mice had increased MRSA burden and duration of carriage compared to SO controls (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Estrogen receptor-α (ERα, encoded by Esr1) signaling increases Th17 cell proliferation and production of IL-17.
source: Estrogen receptor-α (ERα, encoded by Esr1) signaling increases Th17 cell proliferation and production of IL-17 (Fuseini et al., 2019; Newcomb et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on ERα signaling.

claim: Esr1 was expressed in cecal-colonic immune cells.
source: We confirmed Esr1 was expressed in cecal-colonic immune cells, and that it displayed a nonsignificant trend suggesting an increase upon MRSA inoculation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Female Esr1-/- mice had increased MRSA burden compared to heterozygous littermates.
source: Female Esr1-/- mice had increased MRSA burden compared to heterozygous littermates (Figure 6C), indicating that estrogen mediates the enhanced colonization resistance in female mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Estrogen mediates the enhanced colonization resistance in female mice.
source: Female Esr1-/- mice had increased MRSA burden compared to heterozygous littermates (Figure 6C), indicating that estrogen mediates the enhanced colonization resistance in female mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Esr1 knockout experiments showing loss of colonization resistance.

claim: XY(-Sry) gonadal female mice lose MRSA carriage analogous to XX females.
source: We found that XY(-Sry) gonadal female mice lose MRSA carriage analogous to XX females, consistent with prior studies showing that they display similar estradiol levels (Palaszynski et al., 2005; Sasidhar et al., 2012), and both XY and XX(+Sry) gonadal male mice remain persistently colonized at similar levels (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: XY(-Sry) gonadal female mice display similar estradiol levels to XX females.
source: We found that XY(-Sry) gonadal female mice lose MRSA carriage analogous to XX females, consistent with prior studies showing that they display similar estradiol levels (Palaszynski et al., 2005; Sasidhar et al., 2012), and both XY and XX(+Sry) gonadal male mice remain persistently colonized at similar levels (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on hormone levels in four core genotype mice.

claim: Both XY and XX(+Sry) gonadal male mice remain persistently colonized at similar levels.
source: We found that XY(-Sry) gonadal female mice lose MRSA carriage analogous to XX females, consistent with prior studies showing that they display similar estradiol levels (Palaszynski et al., 2005; Sasidhar et al., 2012), and both XY and XX(+Sry) gonadal male mice remain persistently colonized at similar levels (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There is no change in the proportions of CD4+ T cells in the lamina propria between XX males and XX females with and without MRSA.
source: Like their wild-type counterparts, we do not observe a change in the proportions of CD4+ T cells in the lamina propria between XX males and XX females with and without MRSA (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: XX(-Sry) females displayed an increase in IL17A+CD4+ T cells in the lamina propria compared with XX(+Sry) males 2 dpi MRSA inoculation.
source: Instead, XX(-Sry) females displayed an increase in IL17A+CD4+ T cells in the lamina propria compared with XX(+Sry) males 2 dpi MRSA inoculation (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The effect of female sex on colonization resistance is hormonally mediated rather than dependent on genes present on sex chromosomes.
source: Increase in MRSA burden in OVX or ERα-deficient females and XX (+Sry) gonadal male mice indicate that this effect of the female sex is hormonally mediated rather than dependent on genes present on sex chromosomes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results of ovariectomy, Esr1 knockout, and four core genotype experiments.

claim: GI colonization resistance against MRSA in female mice is dependent on the microbiota and an enhanced Th17 response downstream of sex hormones.
source: Collectively, our results support a model in which GI colonization resistance against MRSA in female mice is dependent on the microbiota and an enhanced Th17 response downstream of sex hormones.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating multiple experimental findings from the study.

claim: ERα signaling increases differentiation and cytokine production of Th1 and Th17 cells.
source: Our results are consistent with studies showing that ERα signaling increases differentiation and cytokine production of Th1 and Th17 cells (Fuseini et al., 2019; Mohammad et al., 2018; Maret et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on ERα signaling effects on T cells.

claim: Higher levels of estrogen characteristic of pregnancy can stimulate immunosuppressive regulatory CD4+ T cell conversion.
source: although higher levels of estrogen characteristic of pregnancy can stimulate immunosuppressive regulatory CD4+ T cell conversion (Tai et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on estrogen effects during pregnancy.

claim: Androgen suppresses lymphoid and neutrophil responses during intradermal infection of mice with S. aureus.
source: Recent work identified a parallel role for the male sex hormone androgen in suppressing lymphoid and neutrophil responses during intradermal infection of mice with S. aureus (Chi et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent published literature on androgen effects.

claim: Introduction of a complex microbiota into GF mice amplified the skin type 17 sex bias in females.
source: In this context, introduction of a complex microbiota into GF mice amplified the skin type 17 sex bias in females (Chi et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on microbiota effects on skin immunity.

claim: Sex biases in neutrophil function, including increased phagocytosis and extracellular trap formation in female mice, have been observed.
source: Sex biases in neutrophil function, including increased phagocytosis and extracellular trap formation in female mice, have been observed (Castleman et al., 2018; Yasuda et al., 2019; Spitzer and Zhang, 1996; Pokhrel et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on sex differences in neutrophil function.

claim: BM neutrophils from female mice have an enhanced ability to kill MRSA ex vivo compared to those from male mice, which was linked to increases in surface CD11b and antimicrobial production.
source: In line with our findings of increased CD11b on intestinal neutrophils isolated from female mice exposed to MRSA, studies examining MRSA skin and soft tissue infections found that BM neutrophils from female mice have an enhanced ability to kill MRSA ex vivo compared to those from male mice, which was linked to increases in surface CD11b and antimicrobial production (Castleman et al., 2018; Pokhrel et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on neutrophil function in MRSA infections.

claim: Colonization resistance against S. aureus in the nares is associated with Th17 cells and neutrophils.
source: Although sex difference was not reported, colonization resistance against S. aureus in the nares is also associated with Th17 cells and neutrophils (Archer et al., 2013; Archer et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on nasal colonization resistance.

claim: Protein A produced by S. aureus binds to the Fcγ portion of immunoglobulins, protecting S. aureus from opsonophagocytic killing.
source: The absence of a sterilizing B cell response may reflect immune evasion strategies such as the bacterially produced Protein A that binds to the Fcγ portion of immunoglobulins, protecting S. aureus from opsonophagocytic killing (Falugi et al., 2013; Pauli et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on S. aureus immune evasion.

claim: Antibodies prior to intranasal inoculation did not block persistent colonization by cognate S. aureus strains in a human volunteer study.
source: Our finding that female mice lacking mature B cells were still able to resist MRSA GI colonization is mirrored by a human volunteer study demonstrating that antibodies prior to intranasal inoculation did not block persistent colonization by their cognate S. aureus strains and that antibody levels did not distinguish intermittent and noncarriers (van Belkum et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a human volunteer study.

claim: Low CD4+ T cell counts in HIV+ individuals are a risk factor for S. aureus nasal colonization.
source: In contrast, low CD4+ T cell counts in HIV+ individuals are a risk factor for S. aureus nasal colonization (de Ferreira et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on HIV and S. aureus colonization.

claim: Rates of S. aureus colonization were higher in HIV+ males compared to HIV+ females.
source: and rates of colonization were higher in HIV+ males compared to HIV+ females (Neupane et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on sex differences in HIV+ individuals.

claim: Superantigens from S. aureus bind directly to Vβ regions of T cell receptors (TCRs) and MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells, resulting in hyperactivation of T lymphocytes and monocytes/macrophages.
source: Superantigens from S. aureus bind directly to Vβ regions of T cell receptors (TCRs) and MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells, resulting in hyperactivation of T lymphocytes and monocytes/macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge on superantigen function.

claim: S. aureus superantigens induce a robust IL-17 response from memory Th17 cells from adult humans but not from naive T cells.
source: S. aureus superantigens induce a robust IL-17 response from memory Th17 cells from adult humans but not from naive T cells (Islander et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on superantigen effects on Th17 cells.

claim: CD4+ T cells in the gut, including Th17 cells, can recognize antigens that are shared by taxonomically diverse bacteria in the gut.
source: Also, CD4+ T cells in the gut, including Th17 cells, can recognize antigens that are shared by taxonomically diverse bacteria in the gut (Nagashima et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on gut T cell antigen recognition.

claim: MHC-II restricted CD4+ T cells with Th17 functionality have been identified in the colon of healthy humans and mice that are responsive to commensal microbial antigens in an innate-like manner.
source: In the colon of healthy humans and mice, MHC-II restricted CD4+ T cells with Th17 functionality have been identified that are responsive to commensal microbial antigens in an innate-like manner (Hackstein et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on innate-like Th17 cells.

claim: Intestinal colonization by the fungus Candida albicans favors Th17 polarization associated with increased IL-17 and neutrophils that protect mice from intravenous infection with MRSA.
source: Additionally, intestinal colonization by the fungus Candida albicans favors Th17 polarization associated with increased IL-17 and neutrophils that protect mice from intravenous infection with MRSA (Shao et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on C. albicans effects on immunity.

claim: Investigating the antigen-specific response to MRSA is challenging due to bacterially encoded superantigens and other secreted virulence factors that induce cell death of lymphocytes.
source: Investigating the antigen-specific response to MRSA is challenging due to bacterially encoded superantigens and other secreted virulence factors, such as α-hemolysin and LukED, that induce cell death of lymphocytes (Tam and Torres, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on MRSA virulence factors.

claim: Initial microbiota differences prime the gut for a Th17 and neutrophil response to MRSA that is enhanced by estrogen.
source: However, given the strong connection between microbiota and Th17 (Ivanov et al., 2009; Atarashi et al., 2015), we propose a speculative model in which initial microbiota differences prime the gut for a Th17 and neutrophil response to MRSA that is enhanced by estrogen.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors based on their findings and cited literature.
